questions.q: What is "environment strategy," as this lesson defines it?
options: The architectural decision of how many Salesforce environments to maintain, what each is for, and how work promotes between them safely
A Salesforce product you purchase and install from the AppExchange
The specific Apex design pattern used inside triggers
A setting in Setup that automatically creates sandboxes on a schedule
questions.explain: Environment strategy is a design decision architects make and justify, not a product or a single setting -- it covers how many environments exist, their purpose, and how changes move between them.

questions.q: In the promotion path described in this lesson (Development -> Testing -> Staging -> Production), what is the underlying principle that governs it?
options: Every environment should have identical data at all times
Development environments should always contain full production data to be useful
Changes are only promoted after validation in the prior stage, and the environment closest to production should resemble production the most closely
Staging and testing can be skipped as long as a developer is confident in the change
questions.explain: The promotion path exists specifically so nothing reaches production until it has survived validation in earlier stages, with later stages resembling production more closely than earlier ones.

questions.q: What distinguishes a metadata-only environment from one that also carries data?
options: A metadata-only environment carries configuration (objects, fields, Flows, Apex) but no real records, while a data-carrying environment also includes some or all of production's actual records
A metadata-only environment cannot contain any Apex code
There is no real distinction -- all Salesforce environments carry identical data
Metadata-only environments are only available in Developer Edition orgs
questions.explain: The split is specifically about whether real records are copied in, which matters because some testing (like performance against realistic data volumes) is only meaningful with actual data present.

questions.q: Why does this lesson frame environment strategy as an architect-level decision rather than a routine admin task?
options: Because admins are not permitted to create sandboxes under any circumstance
Because only architects are allowed to log into a sandbox
Because environment strategy never needs to be revisited once set
Because it requires balancing development speed, testing quality, data risk, and license cost against each other as the org and team grow -- not just clicking through a creation form
questions.explain: Creating a single sandbox is simple; deciding how many environments to maintain, who gets access, refresh cadence, and promotion rules involves real trade-offs in cost and risk that architects are expected to own.

questions.q: A 12-person team shares one sandbox for all building, testing, and training. Per this lesson's framing, what is the most likely consequence as the team grows?
options: Nothing changes -- a single shared sandbox scales indefinitely regardless of team size
Conflicting, simultaneous uses of the same environment by different people for different purposes become increasingly likely to interfere with each other
The sandbox will automatically split itself into multiple environments once enough users are added
Salesforce will prevent more than 12 users from ever accessing the same sandbox
questions.explain: A single shared environment works until different people need it for different, conflicting purposes at the same time -- exactly the scaling problem this lesson's lab asks you to reason through.
